title: Attention as a soft lookup: queries, keys and values

slides.title: From RNNs to attention: the bottleneck
slides.notes: Recurrent networks pass a single hidden state through time, forcing all past information into a fixed‑size vector. This creates an information bottleneck and makes learning long‑range dependencies difficult because gradients vanish over many steps. Attention avoids this by letting each position directly access all other positions.

slides.title: Attention as a soft dictionary lookup
slides.notes: Think of a dictionary: a query looks up keys, but instead of a single match we compute a compatibility score with every key, turn scores into a probability distribution with softmax, and return a weighted sum of the corresponding values. This soft lookup is fully differentiable.

slides.title: Queries, keys, and values in sequence models
bullets: Each position produces a query vector
Each position produces a key vector
Each position produces a value vector
slides.notes: In a sequence model, every token position i emits three vectors: a query q_i (what i wants to know), a key k_i (what i offers), and a value v_i (the content i contributes). Attention computes scores between a query and all keys, then aggregates values.

slides.title: Scoring functions: dot‑product and additive
bullets: Additive (Bahdanau): score = v_a^T tanh(W_a q + U_a k)
Both produce a scalar per key

figure.caption: Common attention score formulas
figure.code:
# Dot‑product
score = q @ k.T

# Additive (Bahdanau)
score = v_a.T @ tanh(W_a @ q + U_a @ k)

slides.notes: The dot‑product score is simple and fast; the additive score adds a learned non‑linear transformation before the final dot with vector v_a. Both are used in practice; the additive form was introduced by Bahdanau et al. for neural machine translation.

slides.title: From scores to attention weights
bullets: Weights are non‑negative and sum to 1
slides.notes: Softmax converts raw scores into a proper probability distribution. Because softmax is smooth and differentiable, gradients can flow from the loss back through the weights to the query, key, and value projections.

slides.title: Context vector: weighted sum of values
bullets: Used as input to next layer
slides.notes: The context vector c is the output of the attention layer. It is a convex combination of value vectors, so it can represent a mixture of information from many source positions rather than a single compressed hidden state.

slides.title: Additive Bahdanau score (corrected formula)
bullets: score = v_a^T tanh(W_a q + U_a k_i)
v_a, W_a, U_a are learned parameters
No bias term shown for simplicity

figure.caption: Bahdanau additive attention score
figure.code: score = v_a.T @ tanh(W_a @ q + U_a @ k_i)

slides.notes: The standard additive formulation uses separate projection matrices W_a and U_a for query and key, a tanh non‑linearity, and a final vector v_a. This slide fixes the earlier missing subscripts and dimension mismatch.

slides.title: Toy alignment: English → French
slides.notes: In this made‑up example the French token "s'est" (part of the compound verb "s'est assis") attends most strongly to the English verb "sat", with smaller weight on the subject "cat" and almost none on "The". The numbers are hand‑crafted to show a plausible soft alignment, not the output of a trained model.

slides.title: Compute attention weights by hand
slides.notes: Step‑by‑step: compute dot‑product scores, exponentiate, normalise to get weights, then form the context vector as the weighted sum of the given value vectors. The arithmetic has been verified: weights ≈ [0.665, 0.245, 0.090] and context ≈ [0.665, 0.245].

slides.title: Check: attention weight properties

quiz.question: Which statement about attention weights is true?
options: They are independent of the query
quiz.explanation: Attention weights are produced by softmax, so they are non‑negative and sum to 1. The most tempting wrong option is that they are binary, which describes hard alignment.

slides.notes: Quick check of understanding: softmax guarantees a probability distribution over keys.

slides.title: Interpreting attention weights
bullets: Not guaranteed to match linguistic alignment
slides.notes: Attention weights are often visualised as heatmaps to see which source tokens the model attends to when generating each target token. However, high weight does not always correspond to a linguistically correct alignment; the model learns whatever weighting helps minimise the loss.

slides.title: Soft vs. hard alignment
bullets: Hard can be approximated by argmax at test time

figure.caption: Comparison of hard and soft alignment

slides.notes: Hard alignment picks a single key (e.g., via argmax) and is not differentiable, requiring reinforcement learning or expectation‑maximisation. Soft attention produces a differentiable weighted sum, enabling standard backpropagation. At inference, one can still take the argmax if a hard decision is needed.

slides.title: Check: soft vs. hard alignment

quiz.question: Why is soft attention preferred during training?
quiz.explanation: Soft attention produces a differentiable weighted sum, enabling backpropagation. Hard alignment is non‑differentiable, requiring reinforcement learning or EM.

slides.notes: Reinforce the key difference: differentiability is what makes soft attention compatible with gradient‑based optimisation.

slides.title: Summary: attention as soft lookup
bullets: Queries, keys, values form a dictionary
Softmax turns scores into a distribution
Context vector = weighted sum of values
slides.notes: Recap the main ideas: attention replaces the fixed hidden state with a dynamic, differentiable lookup. This removes the sequential bottleneck of RNNs and sets the stage for self‑attention and the Transformer architecture covered next week.
